item.title: Orthogonal vs symmetric matrices
item.description:
Symmetric Matrices

A real square matrix A∈Rn×nA \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}A∈Rn×n is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

A=AT A = A^T A=AT

In component form, this means entry Aij=AjiA_{ij} = A_{ji}Aij​=Aji​ for all indices i,ji, ji,j. Geometrically, the entries are mirrored across the main diagonal.

Key Properties

  • Real Eigenvalues: All eigenvalues of a real symmetric matrix are guaranteed to be real numbers (λ∈R\lambda \in \mathbb{R}λ∈R).
  • Orthogonal Eigenspaces: Eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are mutually orthogonal. If Av1=λ1v1A v_1 = \lambda_1 v_1Av1​=λ1​v1​ and Av2=λ2v2A v_2 = \lambda_2 v_2Av2​=λ2​v2​ with λ1≠λ2\lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2λ1​=λ2​, then v1⋅v2=0v_1 \cdot v_2 = 0v1​⋅v2​=0.
  • Spectral Theorem: Every real symmetric matrix can be orthogonally diagonalized: A=QΛQT A = Q \Lambda Q^T A=QΛQT where QQQ is an orthogonal matrix composed of normalized eigenvectors, and Λ\LambdaΛ is a diagonal matrix containing the real eigenvalues.
  • Geometric Action: Acting as a linear transformation x↦Axx \mapsto Axx↦Ax, a symmetric matrix stretches or compresses space along a set of mutually perpendicular axes (its eigenvectors) without introducing any shear or rotation relative to those axes.

Orthogonal Matrices

A real square matrix Q∈Rn×nQ \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}Q∈Rn×n is orthogonal if multiplying it by its transpose yields the identity matrix:

QTQ=QQT=I Q^T Q = Q Q^T = I QTQ=QQT=I

This directly implies that the transpose is the inverse:

Q−1=QT Q^{-1} = Q^T Q−1=QT

The columns (and rows) of QQQ form an orthonormal basis of Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn. If the columns are q1,q2,…,qnq_1, q_2, \dots, q_nq1​,q2​,…,qn​:

  • Unit length: ∥qi∥=1\Vert{}q_i\Vert{} = 1∥qi​∥=1 for all iii.
  • Pairwise perpendicular: qi⋅qj=0q_i \cdot q_j = 0qi​⋅qj​=0 whenever i≠ji \neq ji=j.
Rotation by θ in 2D:
Q = [ cos θ -sin θ ]
[ sin θ cos θ ]

Key Properties

  • Isometry (Preserves Geometry): Orthogonal transformations preserve vector lengths and inner products (angles): ∥Qx∥=∥x∥,(Qx)⋅(Qy)=x⋅y \Vert{}Qx\Vert{} = \Vert{}x\Vert{}, \quad (Qx) \cdot (Qy) = x \cdot y ∥Qx∥=∥x∥,(Qx)⋅(Qy)=x⋅y
  • Determinant: det⁡(Q)=±1\det(Q) = \pm 1det(Q)=±1.
    • If det⁡(Q)=+1\det(Q) = +1det(Q)=+1, QQQ represents a pure rotation (orientation-preserving).
      • If det⁡(Q)=−1\det(Q) = -1det(Q)=−1, QQQ represents a reflection or a roto-reflection (orientation-reversing).
  • Eigenvalues on the Unit Circle: The complex eigenvalues of QQQ have an absolute value of 1 (∣λ∣=1\vert{}\lambda\vert{} = 1∣λ∣=1), taking the form eiθe^{i\theta}eiθ.
  • Closure: The product of two orthogonal matrices is also orthogonal ((Q1Q2)T(Q1Q2)=I(Q_1 Q_2)^T (Q_1 Q_2) = I(Q1​Q2​)T(Q1​Q2​)=I), forming the orthogonal group O(n)\text{O}(n)O(n).

Comparison & Interconnection

Property Symmetric Matrix (A=A⊤A=A^\topA=A⊤) Orthogonal Matrix (Q⊤Q=IQ^\top Q=IQ⊤Q=I)
Inverse No simple formula (requires inversion algorithm) Trivial: Q−1=Q⊤Q^{-1}=Q^\topQ−1=Q⊤
Eigenvalues Always real (λ∈R\lambda\in\mathbb{R}λ∈R) Complex numbers on unit circle (∣λ∣=1\lvert\lambda\rvert=1∣λ∣=1)
Geometric Effect Scaling along perpendicular axes Rigid motion: rotations and reflections
Preserves Norm? No (scales vectors by eigenvalues) Yes (∥Qx∥=∥x∥\lVert Qx\rVert=\lVert x\rVert∥Qx∥=∥x∥)

How They Connect

The Spectral Theorem links both concepts directly: any real symmetric matrix AAA can be decomposed using an orthogonal matrix QQQ:

A=QΛQT A = Q \Lambda Q^T A=QΛQT

Here, QQQ rotates coordinate axes to align with the matrix’s principal directions, Λ\LambdaΛ stretches or scales along those axes, and QTQ^TQT rotates them back.

item.title: PCA
item.description:
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is an unsupervised linear dimensionality reduction technique. It transforms a large set of correlated variables into a smaller set of uncorrelated variables called principal components, while retaining as much variance (information) as possible.

The Core Intuition

Imagine holding a 3D object—like a teapot—in front of a lamp so its shadow falls on a wall. Depending on how you rotate the teapot, the 2D shadow might look like a featureless blob, or it might clearly show the spout, handle, and body.

PCA mathematically rotates your high-dimensional data cloud to find the angle that casts the widest, clearest “shadow.” In data terms:

  • Maximum spread equals maximum information: Where data points are spread out the most (highest variance), the differences between them are preserved.
  • Minimum spread equals noise or redundancy: Dimensions where points barely vary are discarded with minimal loss of information.

How PCA Works Step-by-Step

Given a dataset XXX with nnn observations and ppp features:

  1. Standardization (Centering and Scaling) Features often operate on different scales (e.g., age in tens vs. income in tens of thousands). PCA is sensitive to scale, so each feature is standardized to have a mean of 000 and a standard deviation of 111: z=x−μσ z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma} z=σx−μ​
  2. Covariance Matrix Computation Calculate the p×pp \times pp×p covariance matrix Σ\SigmaΣ: Σ=1n−1XTX \Sigma = \frac{1}{n-1} X^T X Σ=n−11​XTX This matrix captures how every feature varies relative to every other feature. Off-diagonal elements show whether pairs of variables are positively or negatively correlated.
  3. Eigenvalue Decomposition Solve for the eigenvalues λ\lambdaλ and eigenvectors vvv of the covariance matrix: Σv=λv \Sigma v = \lambda v Σv=λv
    • Eigenvectors define the directions of the new feature space (the principal axes). They are mutually perpendicular (orthogonal), meaning zero correlation exists between them.
      • Eigenvalues quantify the amount of variance carried by each corresponding eigenvector.
  4. Selecting the Principal Components Rank the eigenvectors by their eigenvalues in descending order:
    • PC1: The axis capturing the single largest variance in the data.
      • PC2: The axis orthogonal to PC1 capturing the next largest variance, and so on. You select the top kkk components that explain a target threshold of total variance (commonly 80% to 95%).
  5. Projecting onto the New Subspace Form a projection matrix WWW using the top kkk eigenvectors and transform the original data XXX into the lower-dimensional representation ZZZ: Z=XW Z = X W Z=XW

Why Use PCA?

  • Visualization: Reduces 10D, 100D, or 10,000D datasets down to 2D or 3D scatter plots to inspect clusters, classes, and outliers.
  • Mitigating the Curse of Dimensionality: Models run faster and require less memory when sparse, high-dimensional inputs are condensed.
  • Removing Multicollinearity: Regressions and linear models struggle with heavily correlated inputs. Principal components are completely orthogonal to each other.
  • Noise Reduction: Discarding lower-variance components often strips out background noise and measurement jitter.

Key Limitations

  • Linear Only: PCA assumes linear relationships between features. For complex manifolds or nonlinear structures, techniques like t-SNE, UMAP, or Kernel PCA are required.
  • Interpretability Trade-off: While the original features had concrete meanings (e.g., “annual salary”, “blood pressure”), principal components are linear combinations of all original features (e.g., 0.42×salary−0.31×pressure0.42 \times \text{salary} - 0.31 \times \text{pressure}0.42×salary−0.31×pressure), making direct attribution harder.
  • Outlier Sensitivity: Because variance is computed using squared distances from the mean, extreme outliers can distort the direction of the principal axes.

item.title: Singular Value Decomposition vs Spectral Value Decomposition
item.description:
Both Spectral Decomposition (also called the Spectral Theorem or Eigendecomposition of symmetric/normal matrices) and Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) factorize a matrix into fundamental geometric operations: rotations, reflections, and scaling along orthogonal axes.

The fundamental distinction lies in scope: Spectral Decomposition applies to square, normal (typically symmetric/Hermitian) matrices using a single orthogonal basis, whereas SVD generalizes this to any m×nm \times nm×n matrix by decoupling input and output coordinate systems.

1. Spectral Decomposition

If AAA is an n×nn \times nn×n real symmetric matrix (A=ATA = A^TA=AT), the Spectral Theorem guarantees that:

  1. All eigenvalues λi\lambda_iλi​ of AAA are real.
  2. Eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are mutually orthogonal.
  3. There exists an orthonormal basis of Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn composed entirely of eigenvectors of AAA.

Mathematical Formulation

A=QΛQT=∑i=1nλiqiqiT A = Q \Lambda Q^T = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i q_i q_i^T A=QΛQT=i=1∑n​λi​qi​qiT​
  • QQQ (n×nn \times nn×n): An orthogonal matrix whose columns q1,…,qnq_1, \dots, q_nq1​,…,qn​ are the orthonormal eigenvectors (QTQ=QQT=IQ^T Q = Q Q^T = IQTQ=QQT=I).
  • Λ\LambdaΛ (n×nn \times nn×n): A diagonal matrix containing the eigenvalues λ1,…,λn\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_nλ1​,…,λn​ along the main diagonal.
  • Outer product expansion: AAA is decomposed into a linear combination of rank-1 orthogonal projection matrices qiqiTq_i q_i^Tqi​qiT​, each scaled by λi\lambda_iλi​.

Geometric Interpretation

Multiplying a vector xxx by AAA decomposes into three steps:

  1. QTxQ^T xQTx: Rotates/reflects xxx into the eigenspace coordinates.
  2. Λ(QTx)\Lambda (Q^T x)Λ(QTx): Scales each coordinate independently by its eigenvalue λi\lambda_iλi​ (can stretch, compress, or reverse direction if λi<0\lambda_i < 0λi​<0).
  3. Q(… )Q (\dots)Q(…): Rotates/reflects the vector back to the original standard basis.

Because the domain and codomain are the exact same space (Rn→Rn\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^nRn→Rn), the input coordinate system and output coordinate system are identical (QTQ^TQT on the right, QQQ on the left).

2. Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)

SVD relaxes the symmetry and square constraints entirely. Any arbitrary real matrix A∈Rm×nA \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}A∈Rm×n can be factored using two distinct orthogonal coordinate systems.

Mathematical Formulation

A=UΣVT=∑i=1rσiuiviT A = U \Sigma V^T = \sum_{i=1}^r \sigma_i u_i v_i^T A=UΣVT=i=1∑r​σi​ui​viT​
  • UUU (m×mm \times mm×m): Orthogonal matrix whose columns uiu_iui​ are the left-singular vectors (orthonormal eigenvectors of AATA A^TAAT).
  • Σ\SigmaΣ (m×nm \times nm×n): Rectangular diagonal matrix containing singular values σ1≥σ2≥⋯≥σr>0\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_r > 0σ1​≥σ2​≥⋯≥σr​>0, followed by zeros.
  • VVV (n×nn \times nn×n): Orthogonal matrix whose columns viv_ivi​ are the right-singular vectors (orthonormal eigenvectors of ATAA^T AATA).
  • rrr: The rank of AAA (r≤min⁡(m,n)r \le \min(m, n)r≤min(m,n)).

Geometric action of SVD. Source: Made with Google AI

Geometric Interpretation

Any linear transformation maps an nnn-dimensional unit hyper-sphere into an mmm-dimensional hyper-ellipse:

  1. VTV^TVT: Rotates the input space Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn so that the right-singular vectors viv_ivi​ align with standard coordinate axes.
  2. Σ\SigmaΣ: Stretches/shrinks the axes by non-negative scale factors σi\sigma_iσi​. If m≠nm \neq nm=n, it embeds or projects into Rm\mathbb{R}^mRm.
  3. UUU: Rotates the resulting hyper-ellipse into its final orientation in the output space Rm\mathbb{R}^mRm, aligning its semi-axes with uiu_iui​.

3. Key Relationships & Differences

Property Spectral Decomposition (QΛQ⊤Q\Lambda Q^\topQΛQ⊤) Singular Value Decomposition (UΣV⊤U\Sigma V^\topUΣV⊤)
Matrix Applicability Square (n×nn\times nn×n), Symmetric (A=A⊤A=A^\topA=A⊤) Any Matrix (m×nm\times nm×n)
Bases Involved One orthonormal basis (QQQ) Two distinct orthonormal bases (UUU and VVV)
Diagonal Values Eigenvalues λi∈R\lambda_i\in\mathbb{R}λi​∈R (can be negative or zero) Singular values σi≥0\sigma_i\ge 0σi​≥0 (strictly non-negative)
Subspace Mapping Maps Rn→Rn\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^nRn→Rn using same axes Maps Rn→Rm\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^mRn→Rm across different dimensions
Connection to Gram Matrices AAA diagonalizes itself directly VVV diagonalizes A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A; UUU diagonalizes AA⊤AA^\topAA⊤

The Exact Connection Between Them

When AAA is symmetric:

  • The singular values are the absolute values of the eigenvalues: σi=∣λi∣\sigma_i = \vert{}\lambda_i\vert{}σi​=∣λi​∣.
  • The right-singular vectors viv_ivi​ correspond to the eigenvectors qiq_iqi​.
  • The left-singular vectors satisfy ui=sign⁡(λi)qiu_i = \operatorname{sign}(\lambda_i) q_iui​=sign(λi​)qi​.

For an arbitrary matrix AAA, SVD can be viewed as computing the spectral decomposition of the symmetric positive semi-definite matrices ATAA^T AATA and AATA A^TAAT:

ATA=(VΣTUT)(UΣVT)=V(ΣTΣ)VT A^T A = (V \Sigma^T U^T)(U \Sigma V^T) = V (\Sigma^T \Sigma) V^T ATA=(VΣTUT)(UΣVT)=V(ΣTΣ)VTAAT=(UΣVT)(VΣTUT)=U(ΣΣT)UT A A^T = (U \Sigma V^T)(V \Sigma^T U^T) = U (\Sigma \Sigma^T) U^T AAT=(UΣVT)(VΣTUT)=U(ΣΣT)UT

Here, the eigenvalues of ATAA^T AATA (and AATA A^TAAT) are precisely σi2\sigma_i^2σi2​, and their orthonormal eigenvectors yield VVV and UUU respectively.

item.title: Spectral theorem
item.description:
The Spectral Theorem is a fundamental result in linear algebra and functional analysis that establishes when an operator or matrix can be diagonalized using an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors.

Geometrically, it means that under the right conditions, a linear transformation is simply a combination of independent stretches along mutually perpendicular axes.

Finite-Dimensional Formulations

Depending on whether you work over real numbers or complex numbers, the theorem takes slightly different forms:

1. Real Symmetric Matrices

If A∈Rn×nA \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}A∈Rn×n is a real symmetric matrix (A=ATA = A^TA=AT):

  • All eigenvalues of AAA are real numbers.
  • Eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are mutually orthogonal.
  • AAA can be factored as: A=QΛQT A = Q \Lambda Q^T A=QΛQT where QQQ is an orthogonal matrix (QTQ=IQ^T Q = IQTQ=I) whose columns are orthonormal eigenvectors of AAA, and Λ\LambdaΛ is a diagonal matrix containing the real eigenvalues λ1,λ2,…,λn\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \dots, \lambda_nλ1​,λ2​,…,λn​.

2. Complex Normal Matrices

If A∈Cn×nA \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}A∈Cn×n, the theorem generalizes to normal matrices, defined by AA∗=A∗AA A^* = A^* AAA∗=A∗A (where A∗A^*A∗ is the conjugate transpose). This family includes Hermitian (A=A∗A = A^*A=A∗), skew-Hermitian (A=−A∗A = -A^*A=−A∗), and unitary (A∗A=IA^* A = IA∗A=I) matrices:

  • AAA is unitarily diagonalizable: A=UΛU∗ A = U \Lambda U^* A=UΛU∗ where UUU is a unitary matrix (U∗U=IU^* U = IU∗U=I) and Λ\LambdaΛ is diagonal.
  • If AAA is specifically Hermitian (A=A∗A = A^*A=A∗), all its eigenvalues are strictly real, mirroring the real symmetric case.

Spectral Decomposition (Projection Form)

Instead of matrix products, the spectral theorem can be written as a sum of one-dimensional orthogonal projections:

A=∑i=1nλiPi A = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i P_i A=i=1∑n​λi​Pi​

where each Pi=uiui∗P_i = u_i u_i^*Pi​=ui​ui∗​ is the projection operator onto the eigenspace spanned by the orthonormal eigenvector uiu_iui​. These projections satisfy:

  • PiPj=0P_i P_j = 0Pi​Pj​=0 for i≠ji \neq ji=j (mutually orthogonal)
  • Pi2=PiP_i^2 = P_iPi2​=Pi​ (idempotent)
  • ∑i=1nPi=I\sum_{i=1}^{n} P_i = I∑i=1n​Pi​=I (resolution of the identity)

This representation makes it trivial to compute powers, inverses, and functions of matrices:

f(A)=∑i=1nf(λi)Pi f(A) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} f(\lambda_i) P_i f(A)=i=1∑n​f(λi​)Pi​

Infinite-Dimensional Extension (Hilbert Spaces)

In quantum mechanics and functional analysis, the theorem extends to bounded (and unbounded) self-adjoint operators TTT on a Hilbert space H\mathcal{H}H.

Because infinite-dimensional operators may possess continuous spectra (where eigenvalues in the discrete sense do not exist, like the position or momentum operators in quantum physics), the summation becomes an integral against a projection-valued measure EEE:

T=∫σ(T)λ dE(λ) T = \int_{\sigma(T)} \lambda \, dE(\lambda) T=∫σ(T)​λdE(λ)

where σ(T)\sigma(T)σ(T) denotes the spectrum of TTT.

Core Applications

  • Principal Component Analysis (PCA): Diagonalizes the symmetric covariance matrix to find principal directions of maximal variance.
  • Singular Value Decomposition (SVD): SVD applies the spectral theorem to ATAA^T AATA and AATA A^TAAT to decompose arbitrary rectangular matrices.
  • Quantum Mechanics: Physical observables correspond to self-adjoint operators. The spectral theorem ensures that measurement outcomes (eigenvalues) are real and that the eigenstates form a complete basis for the state space.
  • Graph Theory: Spectral graph theory uses the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian or adjacency matrix to analyze graph connectivity, clustering, and cuts.

item.title: Tensors
item.description:
At its core, a tensor is a geometric object that maps geometric entities (vectors and covectors) linearly to real numbers, retaining its physical identity regardless of the coordinate system chosen to describe it.

While computer science views tensors merely as multi-dimensional arrays, physics and mathematics define them by how their components transform under a change of basis.

1. Dual Spaces, Vectors, and Covectors

To understand tensors formally, we start on a vector space VVV of dimension nnn over R\mathbb{R}R:

  • Contravariant Vectors (Tangent Vectors, VVV): Elements of VVV. If {eμ}\{e_\mu\}{eμ​} forms a basis of VVV, a vector vvv is represented with an upper index: v=vμeμ v = v^\mu e_\mu v=vμeμ​
  • Covariant Vectors / 1-Forms / Covectors (V∗V^*V∗): Linear functions mapping V→RV \to \mathbb{R}V→R. If {θν}\{\theta^\nu\}{θν} is the dual basis satisfying θν(eμ)=δμν\theta^\nu(e_\mu) = \delta^\nu_\muθν(eμ​)=δμν​, a 1-form ω∈V∗\omega \in V^*ω∈V∗ is written with a lower index: ω=ωνθν \omega = \omega_\nu \theta^\nu ω=ων​θν

Under a coordinate transformation xμ→x′μx^\mu \to x'^\muxμ→x′μ:

  • Tangent vectors transform via the Jacobian matrix: v′μ=∂x′μ∂xαvα v'^\mu = \frac{\partial x'^\mu}{\partial x^\alpha} v^\alpha v′μ=∂xα∂x′μ​vα
  • Dual vectors (gradients of scalars, 1-forms) transform via the inverse Jacobian: ωμ′=∂xα∂x′μωα \omega'_\mu = \frac{\partial x^\alpha}{\partial x'^\mu} \omega_\alpha ωμ′​=∂x′μ∂xα​ωα​

2. General Tensor Definition

A tensor of type (r,s)(r, s)(r,s) (rank r+sr+sr+s) is a multilinear map:

T:V∗×⋯×V∗⏟r copies×V×⋯×V⏟s copies⟶R T: \underbrace{V^* \times \dots \times V^*}_{r \text{ copies}} \times \underbrace{V \times \dots \times V}_{s \text{ copies}} \longrightarrow \mathbb{R} T:r copiesV∗×⋯×V∗​​×s copiesV×⋯×V​​⟶R
  • rrr is the contravariant rank (number of upper indices).
  • sss is the covariant rank (number of lower indices).

Transformation Law

A tensor TTT of type (r,s)(r, s)(r,s) transforms under coordinate change x→x′x \to x'x→x′ as:

T′ν1…νsμ1…μr=(∂x′μ1∂xα1…∂x′μr∂xαr)(∂xβ1∂x′ν1…∂xβs∂x′νs)Tβ1…βsα1…αr {T'}^{\mu_1 \dots \mu_r}_{\nu_1 \dots \nu_s} = \left(\frac{\partial x'^{\mu_1}}{\partial x^{\alpha_1}} \dots \frac{\partial x'^{\mu_r}}{\partial x^{\alpha_r}}\right) \left(\frac{\partial x^{\beta_1}}{\partial x'^{\nu_1}} \dots \frac{\partial x^{\beta_s}}{\partial x'^{\nu_s}}\right) T^{\alpha_1 \dots \alpha_r}_{\beta_1 \dots \beta_s} T′ν1​…νs​μ1​…μr​​=(∂xα1​∂x′μ1​​…∂xαr​∂x′μr​​)(∂x′ν1​∂xβ1​​…∂x′νs​∂xβs​​)Tβ1​…βs​α1​…αr​​

This transformation rule is the operational litmus test: an array of numbers is a tensor if and only if its components transform strictly according to this multilinear law.

3. Essential Tensor Algebra

Einstein Summation Convention

Repeated upper and lower indices imply summation over the dimension range (111 to nnn or 000 to 333):

AμBμ≡∑μ=1nAμBμ A^\mu B_\mu \equiv \sum_{\mu=1}^n A^\mu B_\mu AμBμ​≡μ=1∑n​AμBμ​

Tensor Product (⊗\otimes⊗)

Combines a tensor of type (r,s)(r, s)(r,s) and (p,q)(p, q)(p,q) into a tensor of type (r+p,s+q)(r+p, s+q)(r+p,s+q):

(A⊗B)ν1…νsβ1…βqμ1…μrα1…αp=Aν1…νsμ1…μrBβ1…βqα1…αp (A \otimes B)^{\mu_1 \dots \mu_r \alpha_1 \dots \alpha_p}_{\nu_1 \dots \nu_s \beta_1 \dots \beta_q} = A^{\mu_1 \dots \mu_r}_{\nu_1 \dots \nu_s} B^{\alpha_1 \dots \alpha_p}_{\beta_1 \dots \beta_q} (A⊗B)ν1​…νs​β1​…βq​μ1​…μr​α1​…αp​​=Aν1​…νs​μ1​…μr​​Bβ1​…βq​α1​…αp​​

Contraction

Setting an upper index equal to a lower index sums over that coordinate, reducing the tensor’s rank by 2:

Cνμ→contractionCμμ=Tr⁡(C)(a scalar) C^\mu_{\nu} \xrightarrow{\text{contraction}} C^\mu_\mu = \operatorname{Tr}(C) \quad (\text{a scalar}) Cνμ​contraction​Cμμ​=Tr(C)(a scalar)

Metric Tensor (gμνg_{\mu\nu}gμν​)

A symmetric (0,2)(0, 2)(0,2) tensor that defines the inner product on the tangent space and sets the line element:

ds2=gμνdxμdxν ds^2 = g_{\mu\nu} dx^\mu dx^\nu ds2=gμν​dxμdxν

The metric is invertible (gμαgαν=δνμg^{\mu\alpha} g_{\alpha\nu} = \delta^\mu_\nugμαgαν​=δνμ​) and provides a natural isomorphism to raise and lower indices:

vμ=gμνvν,ωμ=gμνων v_\mu = g_{\mu\nu} v^\nu, \qquad \omega^\mu = g^{\mu\nu} \omega_\nu vμ​=gμν​vν,ωμ=gμνων​

4. Tensor Calculus on Curved Manifolds

On curved spaces (or even flat spaces in curvilinear coordinates), the partial derivative of a tensor component, ∂μTν≡∂Tν∂xμ\partial_\mu T^\nu \equiv \frac{\partial T^\nu}{\partial x^\mu}∂μ​Tν≡∂xμ∂Tν​, fails to transform as a tensor because the basis vectors themselves vary from point to point:

∂eα∂xμ≠0 \frac{\partial e_\alpha}{\partial x^\mu} \neq 0 ∂xμ∂eα​​=0

The Covariant Derivative (∇\nabla∇ or ;;;)

To construct a genuine directional derivative that transforms tensorially, we introduce an affine connection Γμνλ\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}Γμνλ​ (the Christoffel symbols):

For a vector vνv^\nuvν:

∇μvν=∂μvν+Γμλνvλ \nabla_\mu v^\nu = \partial_\mu v^\nu + \Gamma^\nu_{\mu\lambda} v^\lambda ∇μ​vν=∂μ​vν+Γμλν​vλ

For a 1-form ων\omega_\nuων​:

∇μων=∂μων−Γμνλωλ \nabla_\mu \omega_\nu = \partial_\mu \omega_\nu - \Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu} \omega_\lambda ∇μ​ων​=∂μ​ων​−Γμνλ​ωλ​

For a general (r,s)(r, s)(r,s) tensor, add a +Γ+\Gamma+Γ term for every contravariant index and a −Γ-\Gamma−Γ term for every covariant index:

∇λTνμ=∂λTνμ+ΓλσμTνσ−ΓλνσTσμ \nabla_\lambda T^\mu_\nu = \partial_\lambda T^\mu_\nu + \Gamma^\mu_{\lambda\sigma} T^\sigma_\nu - \Gamma^\sigma_{\lambda\nu} T^\mu_\sigma ∇λ​Tνμ​=∂λ​Tνμ​+Γλσμ​Tνσ​−Γλνσ​Tσμ​
